rv.q: Crystal prowls the stage in slacks and a loosened tie with ease and perfect timing.
'700 Sundays' is an irresistible blend of Borscht Belt shtick and heartwarming schmaltz.
More than the ample laughs, Crystal's achievement here is in forging a tender connection to everyone who has experienced or even contemplated the loss of a parent.
Crystal hits both your heartstrings and your funny bone.
We’re putty in his expert hands — and that’s the memory we’ll take with us.
The core pleasures of this warmly affectionate portrait of a New York childhood involve nostalgia and sentiment, the sex and violence of today’s Broadway.
But Crystal pushes the sentimentality so hard that it sometimes seems to break through the other side of the schmaltz-time continuum.
Fortunately, any hints of self-conscious, kumbaya-ish social commentary are folded seamlessly into the comedy, which is gently irreverent, endearingly good-natured and, yes, funny.
In a laugh-out-loud - if quite long - revival of his 2004 one-man, autobiographical show 700 Sundays, you can practically hear his heart soaring

Seeing as few of these shows, if any, have surpassed Crystal's heartwarming and hilarious tour de force, it's a pleasure to have it return for a run before the "Les Miz" revival takes over the Imperial Theatre.
Mostly, this is a near-perfect romp through prime ethnic and distinctly New York material: religion, food, family and sports.
To his great credit, he doesn't coast on his credentials. In '700 Sundays,' he delivers the full measure of his talent.
700 Sundays is a memory piece that pretty much remains the warmhearted, moving and extremely funny night out that it was back in 2004.
Crystal does here — and it’s more than enough.

cn.t: Crystal's warmhearted, hilarious memoir about his father and Long Island childhood remains a crowd-pleasing tour de force, blending old-school Jewish humor with genuine sentiment, though some find the shtick overly familiar.

sg.ra: Imperial's auditorium is rectangular and wider than it is deep, so you lose very little distance moving back from the premium C-G band — and once you clear the mezzanine overhang (which hangs over Orchestra row H) the rake picks up enough to see over heads. Multiple Chess (2026) and Water for Elephants (2024) sitters in rows H-P described a dead-center full-stage view at sub-premium prices; one Chess viewer at Orch C H106 called it 'the best broadway seats I've had.' Seatplan, TickPick, and Headout independently pick this same band as the value tier.

TickPick and Seatplan both explicitly recommend Front Mezz row C and back (centered) over rows A-B, because the Imperial's front-mezz railing sits high enough to clip the stage for front-row sitters — a Water for Elephants viewer at Front Mezz R A401 (self-reported 6'3") wrote 'The bar definitely gets in the way… Avoid.' Rows C-F clear that bar while keeping the whole-stage overhead view that's the main reason to choose mezzanine over orchestra at Imperial.

sg.vl: Steep rake saves the cheap seats
sg.ra: Imperial has no elevators/escalators and the rear mezz is a real climb (one Chess sitter called it 'quite the hike'), but the rake is steep enough that several Chess and Smash viewers reported unobstructed full-stage views from rows A-C even with tall people in front ('Rake is good so most likely no heads blocking the stage,' 'Theater has a good rake so you can see over the person in front of you'). TickPick and Headout both specifically recommend rear-mezz center (not sides) as the cheap-seat sweet spot here.

sg.vl: Under the overhang, far from the action
sg.ra: Imperial is wider than it is deep, so the penalty for sitting far back is real — you lose closeness without gaining much sightline, and the same mid-tier price bracket gets you a few rows forward.
